title: III. The Medical Experts And A Pound Of Nuts
paragraphs: The testimony of the medical experts, too, did the prisoner little good. And it turned out later that Fetyukovitch hadn't been counting on it for much. The medical line of defense had only been pursued at Katerina Ivanovna's insistence, since she'd specially sent for a celebrated doctor from Moscow. The defense, of course, stood to lose nothing by it, and might, with luck, gain something. There was, however, a distinctly comic element to it, owing to the doctors' disagreement among themselves. The medical experts were the famous Moscow doctor, our own Doctor Herzenstube, and the young Doctor Varvinsky. The latter two also appeared as witnesses for the prosecution.

The first called as an expert witness was Doctor Herzenstube. He was a gray, bald old man of seventy, of medium height and sturdy build. Everyone in town held him in great esteem and respect. He was a conscientious doctor, an excellent and devout man, a Herrnhuter, or Moravian Brother—I'm not entirely sure which. He'd lived among us for many years and carried himself with remarkable dignity. He was kind-hearted and humane. He treated the poor and the peasants for nothing, visited them in their slums and huts, and left money behind for medicine, but he was as stubborn as a mule. Once an idea had lodged in his head, nothing could shake it loose. Nearly everyone in town knew, incidentally, that the famous Moscow doctor had, within his first two or three days among us, made some extremely insulting remarks about Doctor Herzenstube's competence. Although the Moscow doctor charged twenty-five roubles a visit, several people in town were glad to take advantage of his presence, and rushed to consult him no matter the cost. All of them, naturally, had previously been Doctor Herzenstube's patients, and the celebrated doctor had criticized his treatment with real harshness. In the end, he'd taken to asking each patient the moment he saw them, "Well, who's been stuffing you full of nostrums? Herzenstube? Heh heh!" Doctor Herzenstube, of course, heard about all this, and now all three doctors appeared, one after another, to be examined.

Doctor Herzenstube flatly declared that the abnormality of the prisoner's mental faculties was self-evident. Then, giving his reasons for this opinion, which I'll skip over here, he added that the abnormality wasn't only apparent in many of the prisoner's past actions, but was visible even now, at this very moment. Asked to explain how it was apparent right now, the old doctor, with simple, guileless directness, pointed out that the prisoner, on entering the courtroom, had worn "an extraordinary expression, remarkable given the circumstances"; that he'd "marched in like a soldier, staring straight ahead, though it would have been more natural for him to look to the left, where the ladies were sitting among the public, seeing as he's such a great admirer of the fair sex, and must be very curious what the ladies are saying about him just now," the old man concluded, in his peculiar way of speaking.

I should add that he spoke Russian fluently, but every sentence came out shaped in the German style, which didn't trouble him in the least, since it had always been one of his particular vanities to believe he spoke Russian perfectly—better, in fact, than Russians themselves. He was also very fond of Russian proverbs, always insisting that Russian proverbs were the finest, most expressive sayings in the whole world. I might note, too, that in conversation, through simple absent-mindedness, he often forgot the most ordinary words, which sometimes slipped clean out of his head, even ones he knew perfectly well. The same thing happened when he spoke German, and at such moments he'd always wave a hand in front of his face, as if trying to catch the missing word out of the air, and nothing could persuade him to go on speaking until he'd found it. His remark that the prisoner ought to have looked at the ladies when he entered set off an amused murmur in the audience. All our ladies were quite fond of the old doctor; they also knew that, having spent his whole life a bachelor and a devout man of exemplary conduct, he regarded women as lofty, elevated creatures. So his unexpected remark struck everyone as very odd indeed.

The Moscow doctor, questioned in his turn, repeated firmly and emphatically that he considered the prisoner's mental state abnormal in the highest degree. He spoke at length, and with great erudition, about "aberration" and "mania," arguing that from all the facts gathered, the prisoner had undoubtedly been in a state of mental aberration for several days before his arrest, and that if he had in fact committed the crime, it must, even if he was conscious of it at the time, have been nearly involuntary, since he lacked the power to control the morbid impulse gripping him.

But setting aside temporary aberration, the doctor also diagnosed a mania, which, in his words, threatened to lead to complete insanity down the road. (I should note I'm reporting this in my own words; the doctor himself used highly learned, technical language.) "All his actions run contrary to common sense and logic," he went on. "Setting aside what I haven't personally witnessed—that is, the crime itself and the whole catastrophe—the day before yesterday, while speaking with me, he had an inexplicably fixed look in his eyes. He burst out laughing unexpectedly, when there was nothing at all to laugh at. He showed constant, unaccountable irritability, using strange words—'Bernard!' 'Ethics!'—and others equally out of place." But the doctor detected the mania most clearly, he said, in the fact that the prisoner couldn't even mention the three thousand roubles he believed he'd been cheated out of without extraordinary agitation, even though he could speak comparatively calmly about other misfortunes and grievances. By all accounts, in the past too, whenever the subject of the three thousand roubles came up, he'd fly into an absolute frenzy—and yet he was, by all reports, a man indifferent to money, not at all grasping.

"As for my learned colleague's opinion," the Moscow doctor added, ironically, in closing, "that the prisoner, on entering the courtroom, would naturally have looked at the ladies rather than straight ahead, I'll only say that, setting aside the sheer whimsy of the theory, it's fundamentally unsound. Because while I fully agree that the prisoner, entering the courtroom where his fate is to be decided, wouldn't naturally stare straight ahead in that fixed way, and that this may indeed be a sign of his abnormal mental state, I maintain, at the same time, that he wouldn't naturally look to the left, toward the ladies, but rather to the right, to find his legal counsel, on whose help all his hopes rest, and on whose defense his entire future depends." The doctor delivered his opinion with firm, emphatic conviction.

But it was the unexpected pronouncement of Doctor Varvinsky that added the final touch of comedy to the experts' disagreement. In his opinion, the prisoner was now, and had been all along, in a perfectly normal state, and although he'd certainly been nervous and exceedingly agitated before his arrest, this could be traced to several perfectly obvious causes—jealousy, anger, continual drunkenness, and so on. But this nervous state wouldn't amount to the mental aberration just described. As for whether the prisoner should have looked to the left or the right upon entering the courtroom, "in his modest opinion," the prisoner would naturally look straight ahead on entering, exactly as he had done, since that was where the judges sat, the men on whom his fate depended. So it was precisely by looking straight ahead that he'd shown his perfectly normal state of mind at present. The young doctor closed out his "modest" testimony with a touch of heat.
"Bravo, doctor!" Mitya cried, from his seat. "Exactly so!"

Mitya was, of course, reprimanded, but the young doctor's opinion had a decisive effect on the judges and the public, and, as it turned out later, everyone agreed with him. But Doctor Herzenstube, called as a witness, proved quite unexpectedly useful to Mitya. As a longtime resident of the town who'd known the Karamazov family for years, he offered a few facts of considerable value to the prosecution, and then suddenly, as if recalling something, added:

"But the poor young man might have had a very different life, for he had a good heart both as a child and after childhood—that much I know. But the Russian proverb says, 'One head is good, but if another clever man comes to visit him, it'd be even better, for then there'd be two heads instead of just one.'"

"One head is good, but two are better," the prosecutor put in, impatiently. He knew the old man's habit of speaking slowly and deliberately, indifferent to the impression he made or the delay he caused, and prizing his flat, dull, ever-gleeful German wit far too highly. The old man loved cracking jokes.

"Oh yes, that's just what I say," he went on, stubbornly. "One head is good, but two are much better, only he never met that second clever head, and his wits went astray. Where did they go? I've forgotten the word." He went on, waving his hand in front of his eyes, "Oh, yes—spazieren."
"Wandering?"

"Oh, yes, wandering, that's just what I say. Well, his wits went off wandering and fell into such a deep hole that he lost himself entirely. And yet he was a grateful, sensitive boy. Oh, I remember him very well, a little fellow so high, left neglected by his father in the back yard, running around without shoes on his feet, his little breeches hanging by a single button."
A note of real feeling and tenderness suddenly crept into the honest old man's voice. Fetyukovitch genuinely started, as if catching a scent, and pounced on it at once.

"Oh, yes, I was a young man then.... I was... well, forty-five, I think, and had only just arrived here. And I felt so sorry for the boy at the time; I asked myself, why shouldn't I buy him a pound of... a pound of what? I've forgotten what it's called. A pound of the thing children love so much, what is it, what is it?" The doctor began waving his hands again. "It grows on a tree, it's gathered, and given out to everyone...."
"Apples?"
"Oh, no, no. You buy apples by the dozen, not the pound.... No, there are lots of them, all small. You put them in your mouth and crack them."
"Nuts?"

"Just so, nuts, that's what I'm saying," the doctor repeated, perfectly calm, as if he'd never been at a loss for the word at all. "And I bought him a pound of nuts, because no one had ever bought that boy a pound of nuts before. And I raised my finger and said to him, 'Boy, Gott der Vater.' He laughed and said, 'Gott der Vater.'... 'Gott der Sohn.' He laughed again and lisped, 'Gott der Sohn.' 'Gott der heilige Geist.' Then he laughed and said, as best he could, 'Gott der heilige Geist.' I went off, and two days later I happened to be passing by, and he called out to me on his own, 'Uncle, Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn,' and he'd only forgotten 'Gott der heilige Geist.' But I reminded him, and I felt sorry for him all over again. But then he was taken away, and I never saw him again. Twenty-three years passed. I'm sitting one morning in my study, a white-haired old man, when a blooming young man walks into the room, whom I'd never have recognized, but he raised his finger and said, laughing, 'Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn, and Gott der heilige Geist. I've just arrived, and I've come to thank you for that pound of nuts, because no one else ever bought me a pound of nuts—you're the only one who ever did.' And then I remembered my own happy youth, and the poor child in the yard, with no shoes on his feet, and my heart was touched, and I said, 'You're a grateful young man, for having remembered your whole life the pound of nuts I bought you as a child.' And I embraced him, and blessed him. And I shed tears. He laughed, but he shed tears too... because a Russian will often laugh when he really ought to be weeping. But he did weep, I saw it. And now, alas!..."
"And I'm weeping now too, German, I'm weeping now too, you saintly man," Mitya suddenly cried.

In any case, the story left a certain favorable impression on the public. But the real sensation in Mitya's favor came from Katerina Ivanovna's testimony, which I'll describe directly. Indeed, once the witnesses for the defense began giving their evidence, fortune seemed all at once to turn noticeably in Mitya's favor, and, most strikingly, this came as a surprise even to the defense counsel himself. But before Katerina Ivanovna was called, Alyosha was examined, and he recalled a fact that seemed to offer solid evidence against one important point in the prosecution's case.
